blocks.text: Of the turtledove and the wood pigeon the same Philosopher writes: Ἔχει δὲ τὸν ἄῤῥενα ἡ τρυγὼν τὸν αὐτὸν καὶ φάττα, καὶ ἄλλον οὐ προσίενται [Echei de ton arrhena hē trygōn ton auton kai phatta, kai allon ou prosientai], The turtledove too, and the wood pigeon, have one male, and do not admit another. Indeed, Porphyry, On Abstinence from Animal Food book 3, and Phile, On Animals ch. 19, report that wood pigeons punish adultery with death. Both take this from Aelian, Hist. book 3, ch. 44, where he adds that turtledoves keep the same law scrupulously, but that white doves kill only the males caught in adultery, taking pity on the females. Clement, too, in the second book of the Stromata, reports that there are certain animals ἃ τὴν ἐπιμιξίαν οὐ ποιεῖται πρὸς πολλὰ καὶ ἀναίδην, ἀλλὰ πρὸς ἓν, καὶ ὁμόφυλον· οἷαι αἱ πελειάδες, καὶ αἱ φάσσαι, καὶ τὸ τρυγόνων γένος, καὶ ὅσα τούτοις παραπλήσια [ha tēn epimixian ou poieitai pros polla kai anaidēn, alla pros hen, kai homophylon; hoiai hai peleiades, kai hai phassai, kai to trygonōn genos, kai hosa toutois paraplēsia], which do not mate with many and shamelessly, but with one, and that of the same kind, as are doves, and wood pigeons, and the turtledove kind, and those that are like them. What is more, they say that the black dove remains a widow after the death of its mate, and that for this reason among the Egyptians it was the symbol of a woman who shrinks from a second marriage. Horus book 2, ch. 30: Γυναῖκα χήραν ἐπιμείνασαν ἄχρι θανάτου θέλοντες σημῆναι, περιστερὰν μέλαιναν ζωγραφοῦσιν· αὕτη γὰρ οὐ συμμίγνυται ἑτέρῳ ἀνδρὶ ἕως οὗ χηρεύει [Gynaika chēran epimeinasan achri thanatou thelontes sēmēnai, peristeran melainan zōgraphousin; hautē gar ou symmignytai heterō andri heōs hou chēreuei] When they wish to signify a woman who remains a widow until death, they paint a black dove: for this bird, as long as it is widowed, does not join with another male. Accordingly Tertullian tries to establish his monogamy by the example of the dove: A bird, he says, not only harmless but also chaste, which one male alone knows. But the later Fathers, with great unanimity, transferred this very thing to turtledoves, for what reason I do not know. Origen on the Song of Songs, Homily 2: They say that the nature of turtledoves is such that the male does not approach any female besides one, nor does the female accept more than one male; so that, if it happens that one is taken away and the other survives, the love of mating is extinguished together with the mate. Basil in the Hexaemeron, Homily 8: Τὴν τρυγόνα φασὶ διαζευχθεῖσάν ποτε τοῦ ὁμόζυγος, μηκέτι τὴν πρὸς ἕτερον καταδέχεσθαι κοινωνίαν, ἀλλὰ μένειν ἀσυνδύαστον, μνήμῃ τοῦ ποτε συζευχθέντος τὴν πρὸς ἕτερον κοινωνίαν ἀπαρνημένην· [Tēn trygona phasi diazeuchtheisan pote tou homozygos, mēketi tēn pros heteron katadechesthai koinōnian, alla menein asyndyaston, mnēmē tou pote syzeuchthentos tēn pros heteron koinōnian aparnēmenēn] They say that the turtledove, once separated from its mate, never enters into union with another, but remains single without a mate, refusing marriage with another in remembrance of the partner it has lost. Gregory of Nazianzus in the Precepts to Virgins, Poem 3:

Πυνθάνομ᾽ ὡς πτερόεσσα τρυγὼν τρυγόνος φιλίοιο Χηρωθεῖσ᾽ ὁμόλεκτρον ἑὸν ποθέουσα σαόφρων, Οὐ δέχεται πόσιν ἄλλον ἑῆς καθύπερθε καλιῆς· [Pynthanom᾽ hōs pteroessa trygōn trygonos philioio Chērōtheis᾽ homolektron heon potheousa saophrōn, Ou dechetai posin allon heēs kathyperthe kaliēs]
